record.title: Terminal-Bench audit shows why an all-fail score does not certify task hardness
record.summary: A September 2026 paper audits the frozen Terminal-Bench 3 / Frontier-Bench 0.1 production record to ask what an all-fail score actually supports. It covers 1,081 pull requests, 639 scored tasks and 28,801 trials. Of 125 tasks with no honest pass, an ordered screen retains 78 as certified-unsolved candidates; the other 47 are broken-oracle, infrastructure-limited, exploit-only-passable or unresolved cases. The paper defines certified-unsolved narrowly: a reference route passed, infrastructure did not dominate, no strict verifier bypass was observed, and all evaluated agents failed in the frozen setup. This is not proof of intrinsic hardness or failure at the intended capability. The task-level audit and token-cost analysis are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced here.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The authors published an item-level validity audit of a frozen Terminal-Bench 3 / Frontier-Bench 0.1 task-production record.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the paper's frozen record, 125 tasks had no honest pass. An ordered validity screen retains 78 as certified-unsolved candidates and classifies the remaining 47 as 14 broken-oracle, 8 infrastructure-limited, 4 exploit-only-passable and 21 with uncertified solvability.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Among passing tasks, minimum output tokens to first archived pass separated the authors' broader genuine-hard candidates from tractable tasks with AUC 0.750 (95% CI 0.700–0.801); this is observational, not a measure of intrinsic difficulty.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: Certified-unsolved means one authored route passed, infrastructure did not dominate, no strict bypass was observed, and evaluated agents failed in the frozen setup; it does not prove intrinsic hardness or failure at the intended capability.

evidence_gaps.description: Independent re-adjudication of a stratified sample of all-fail tasks with repeated reference runs, infrastructure checks and reward-independent verifier testing.
Test whether the five-way item-validity screen and observed defect rates transfer to other agentic benchmarks and task-production pipelines.

brief.importance_rationale: If the audit generalizes, separating benchmark item validity from raw pass rates could change how frontier agent results are interpreted and how benchmark maintainers qualify capability claims. The result is material to evaluation practice but comes from one frozen benchmark corpus and remains author-reported.
limitations: All task-level adjudication counts are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced here.
The study uses one frozen benchmark-production corpus and cannot establish how often the same failure categories occur in other agent benchmarks.
Only 25 of the 78 certified-unsolved candidates have at least two recorded oracle runs; a passing reference route does not establish verifier completeness or intrinsic hardness.
The paper says the labels do not imply full domain-expert re-review and some failure trajectories remain unresolved.
The AUC result for first-pass token cost is observational and mixes reasoning, verbosity, tools, retries, harness policy and model assignment.

It covers 1,081 pull requests, 639 scored tasks and 28,801 trials. Of 125 tasks with no honest pass, an ordered screen retains 78 as certified-unsolved candidates; the other 47 are broken-oracle, infrastructure-limited, exploit-only-passable or unresolved cases. The paper defines certified-unsolved narrowly: a reference route passed, infrastructure did not dominate, no strict verifier bypass was observed, and all evaluated agents failed in the frozen setup. This is not proof of intrinsic hardness or failure at the intended capability. The task-level audit and token-cost analysis are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced here.

technical.claimed_result: The frozen corpus contains 1,081 pull requests, 639 scored tasks, 28,801 trials and $105,933 in logged agent spend. Of 125 tasks with no honest pass, 78 survive as certified-unsolved candidates; 14 have broken oracles, 8 are infrastructure-limited, 4 are exploit-only-passable and 21 have uncertified solvability. For passing tasks, token cost to first pass separates broader genuine-hard candidates from tractable tasks with AUC 0.750 (95% CI 0.700–0.801).
technical.compute_or_cost: The authors report $105,933 in logged agent spend for the full frozen record and use output tokens to first pass as an observational effort signal. Neither measure establishes intrinsic difficulty or a causal capability estimate.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv paper, adjudication definitions, task counts, strictness ladder and reported checks are directly inspectable. The analyses and labels are the authors' audit results; they have not been independently reproduced in this review.
technical.implementation_status: Retrospective audit of an existing benchmark production corpus; no new agent model or deployment is reported.
technical.mechanism: The audit joins task packages, reference-solution runs, empty-solution controls, adversarial trials, trajectories, telemetry and review records, then applies an ordered screen for reference-route validity, infrastructure dominance and reward-independent verifier bypass. It also studies the recorded token cost to first accepted pass among tasks that were solved.
technical.regime: Frozen Terminal-Bench 3 / Frontier-Bench 0.1 production snapshot: 1,081 pull requests, 639 scored tasks and 28,801 trials. The main task-level screen covers 125 tasks with no honest pass. The token-cost analysis covers tasks with at least one honest pass. Results are conditional on the recorded tasks, harnesses, models, provider state and budgets.
technical.reproducibility: The paper identifies a frozen signal-table snapshot and describes controls and task records. This review did not independently retrieve or replay the underlying task-level data; independent re-adjudication remains open.
technical.strongest_baseline: Raw all-fail pass-rate classification, compared with a multi-evidence ordered validity screen; task difficulty among passing items is compared using first-pass token costs.

brief.title: Terminal-Bench audit shows why an all-fail score does not certify task hardness
brief.why_it_matters: A zero pass rate can reflect a capability gap, a broken reference solution, infrastructure failure or a verifier defect. This paper demonstrates an item-level reporting method that keeps those interpretations separate, helping prevent invalid benchmark items from being treated as capability evidence. Its scope is one frozen benchmark corpus and the certification label is deliberately weaker than intrinsic hardness.
